Nearly 60% of aircraft breakdowns can be attributed to turbofan engine failures, underscoring the urgent need for advanced maintenance strategies.
Turbofan engines operate under complex conditions with variations in altitude, temperature, and flight phase, leading to significant distribution shifts between operating scenarios.
Turbofan engine data is high-dimensional, with more sensors required to monitor engine status compared to bearings or batteries, resulting in a complex feature space.
Unlike bearings, which generate high-frequency signals, turbofan engines produce slower-changing signals that reflect overall health rather than immediate conditions.
Domain adaptation offers a promising solution to address the challenges of limited data and distribution shifts caused by varying operating conditions in turbofan engine RUL prediction.
The proposed taxonomy categorizes DA methods into methodology-based, alignment-based, and problem-based approaches to provide a comprehensive framework for analyzing existing works.
Adversarial-based DA methods, such as DANN and ADDA, have demonstrated superior performance in turbofan engine RUL prediction by learning domain-invariant representations.
Adversarial-based methods face limitations in balancing the source domain prediction loss and the domain adaptation loss, which can hinder optimal adaptation.
Fine-tuning and metric-based approaches, such as CORAL and MMD, have also been explored for turbofan engine RUL prediction, offering alternative strategies to adversarial methods.

The review identifies future research directions, including addressing uncertainty, time-varying characteristics, incomplete data, and sensor-level challenges, to enhance the reliability and effectiveness of DA techniques for turbofan engine RUL prediction.
